subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage: Ines had planned the beach day in Cascais for weeks. Early that morning Paulo texted: "Can't. Sorry." No explanation. Ines stared at the screen, stung. When she replied, "Again?", he wrote only, "Yes. Again." She spent the morning drafting angry messages and deleting them. By afternoon she took a tram to his Lisbon flat with a box of custard tarts. Paulo opened the door slowly, one hand pressed to his lower back, face grey. "Bad day," he said. Ines remembered what he had told her months ago: some days the pain took everything, even his words. "I'm not staying long," she said, handing him the box. "I just wanted you to know I'm not cross." His shoulders dropped. "Thanks. Next good day, the beach is on me."

qa.q: What did Ines bring to Paulo's flat?
qa.a: A box of custard tarts.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling after Paulo's short reply?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry, taking the curt "Yes. Again." personally.

qa.q: What choice kept the friendship kind, and why?
qa.a: Ines visited briefly with the tarts and said she was not cross, remembering that pain drains Paulo's energy and even his words.

qa.q: What was the cancelled day like for Paulo?
qa.a: It was a bad pain day that left him grey and short of words, and he seemed relieved that Ines was not cross.

grounding: Shows a friend of someone in constant pain hurt by a cancelled plan and curt replies, then choosing understanding over taking it personally.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage: At the university library, Preeti had booked the group room for the four of them. Gurpreet arrived late, perched on the edge of her chair and snapped, "Can we just get this done?" when Preeti suggested going through the slides again. Preeti's cheeks burned. It was the third time this month Gurpreet had been curt or cancelled. Later, packing up, Preeti noticed Gurpreet standing to take notes, shifting her weight and wincing. She remembered Gurpreet saying in first year that her joint pain never really went away, only got louder some days. At the coffee counter Preeti asked quietly, "Is today a bad pain day?" Gurpreet nodded, eyes wet. "Sorry I bit your head off." "You don't have to be sorry. Next time, shall we meet in the ground-floor room with the softer chairs?"

qa.q: Where does Preeti suggest meeting next time?
qa.a: In the ground-floor room with the softer chairs.

qa.q: What did Preeti feel when Gurpreet snapped?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt; her cheeks burned, since Gurpreet had been curt before.

qa.q: What helped Preeti stay kind instead of taking it personally?
qa.a: Noticing Gurpreet wincing and remembering the long-lasting pain, then asking quietly and offering a more comfortable room.

qa.q: What might the study session have been like for Gurpreet?
qa.a: Painful and draining; sitting hurt, so her patience ran short and she snapped, then felt sorry.

grounding: Illustrates a friend hurt by curt replies and cancellations from someone living with long-lasting pain, and understanding helping her stay kind.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage:
"Charu, you cancelled again? That's three times this month."
"Sorry. Bad day."
"You could've said more than two words. I'd booked the tickets."
"I said sorry, Sid."
"It feels like you don't care anymore."
"That's not it."
"Then what is it?"
"My back. It's been bad since the accident, and some days two hours in a cinema seat is too much. By evening I've got nothing left, not even words."
"Why didn't you tell me it was that bad?"
"Because I'm tired of being the sick friend. People get annoyed."
"I was annoyed. I thought it was about me."
"It's never about you. I just run out of battery."
"Okay. Next time, a film at my place on the laptop? You can lie on the floor if you want."
"I'd like that," Charu said, and for the first time that week, Siddharth heard a smile.

qa.q: What had Siddharth booked?
qa.a: The tickets.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when Charu cancelled?
qa.a: Siddharth felt hurt and annoyed, thinking Charu didn't care anymore.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do that kept the friendship kind?
qa.a: Siddharth asked what was really going on, listened, and suggested a plan that fits the pain, like a film on the laptop at home.

qa.q: Why has Charu been so curt?
qa.a: Charu is drained by constant back pain and tired of being the sick friend, so by evening there is no energy left for words.

grounding: Shows a friend hurt by cancelled plans and curt replies who learns that constant pain drains energy, and adjusts instead of taking it personally.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage: I used to keep a list in my head of every time Vikas let me down. Skipped my birthday. Left the trek halfway. Replied "k" to a long message about my breakup. I'm Mohit, and I was sure he'd outgrown me. Then last winter I went to his house unannounced and found him lying on the floor with a heat pad on his knee, grey-faced, trying to finish an assignment. He'd had joint pain since he was fifteen, and it had got worse at college. He hadn't told me because he didn't want pity. Everything on my list suddenly looked different. "K" wasn't coldness; it was all he could type that day. Now I ask "good day or bad day?" before making plans, and on bad days I bring snacks and we watch cricket from the floor. He still cancels sometimes. It doesn't sting the way it did.

qa.q: What was Vikas lying with on his knee?
qa.a: A heat pad.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel before learning about the pain?
qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and let down, keeping a list and believing Vikas had outgrown the friendship.

qa.q: What small habit helped Mohit stay kind?
qa.a: Asking "good day or bad day?" before plans and adjusting, like bringing snacks and watching cricket from the floor on bad days.

qa.q: Why hadn't Vikas told Mohit about the pain?
qa.a: Vikas didn't want pity, so he hid how much the joint pain was draining him.

grounding: Shows a friend hurt by cancellations and curt replies who learns about the other's long-lasting pain and stops taking it personally.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage:
Counsellor's notes, Wednesday
Himani came in today upset about her friend Omkar. They used to study together every evening; now he cancels most plans and answers her in one-word texts. Yesterday he snapped at her in the library, and she cried in the corridor afterwards, wondering what she had done wrong. She mentioned, almost in passing, that he has been living with back pain since a sports injury last year. We talked about how constant pain can drain patience and energy long before it shows on the outside, and how short replies may say more about his day than about her. She decided to ask him directly what helps on bad days rather than guess. She also said she will keep seeing her other friends so she doesn't carry it alone. I'll see her again in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Omkar do in the library yesterday?
qa.a: He snapped at Himani.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling after crying in the corridor?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, wondering what she had done wrong.

qa.a: Ask Omkar directly what helps on bad days instead of guessing, and keep seeing other friends so she doesn't carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Omkar's days look from the inside?
qa.a: Constant back pain may be draining his energy and patience, so his short replies reflect the pain rather than his feelings for Himani.

grounding: Shows a friend hurt by curt replies and cancelled plans learning that chronic pain drains patience, and choosing to ask rather than take it personally.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage:
Sunday night
Urmila cancelled again, the third time this month. We'd planned the film for two weeks, and at five she sent: 'Sorry, bad pain day, can't.' When I asked if she was sure, she replied, 'Yes, Samir. I'm sure.' Full stop. Ouch. I sat on the hostel steps feeling like I didn't matter.
Then I remembered her face in the canteen on Friday, grey and tight, and how she kept shifting in her chair. She's lived with this back pain since the accident last year. Of course she's short on patience; she's short on everything. I'm not taking it personally. I texted: 'No worries. Want me to bring the film and some chaat to your room next week instead?' She sent back a heart.
Samir

qa.q: What did Samir offer to bring next week?
qa.a: The film and some chaat to Urmila's room.

qa.q: How did Samir feel after Urmila's curt reply?
qa.a: Samir felt hurt and unimportant, sitting on the hostel steps as if not mattering.

qa.q: What helped Samir respond kindly?
qa.a: Remembering Urmila's grey face and shifting in the chair, and understanding that pain drains patience, so it wasn't personal.

qa.q: What might Urmila have felt when Samir offered to come to her room?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and cared for, sending a heart instead of more apologies.
